annotations.title: The Burning of Grace Church
annotations.text:
An ancestral parish, Grace Church, was founded on Powell Street in 1849 by the Rev. Dr. John Ver Mehr, during the California Gold Rush. Grace Chapel was replaced by a larger church in 1851. A year later, an imposing third Grace Church was built, further up the later-named Nob Hill. Grace Church was destroyed in the fire that followed the great 1906 San Francisco earthquake.

The mural depicts that burning of Grace Church, at California and Stockton Streets. A family flees their Nob Hill mansion at left. At right, rector Rev. John Evans and Bishop William Nichols save parish registers and plate. A fireman at left center stands helpless, as the water mains were broken.

annotations.title: AIDS Interfaith Memorial Chapel
annotations.text:
As the AIDS crisis deepened in the early 1990s it was decided to set apart the north tower (also known as the Singing Tower) floor space for a memorial chapel. Inaugurated in 1995, the completed AIDS Interfaith Memorial Chapel was dedicated in 2000. A 2017 redesign brought a calmer more reflective tone to the chapel.

The “centerpiece” of the chapel (left) is the “Life of Christ” tryptich altarpiece by New York pop artist Keith Haring. The bronze and white-gold work depicts a symbolic multiarmed figure of compassion with symbols of the life of Christ (baby, heart, cross) flanked by angels (some departed souls) above a desperate crowd of humanity. It was Haring’s most important religious work, completed just before his own death from AIDS in 1990.

Since the chapel opened a block of the NAMES AIDS Quilt has hung here (right), rotated a few times a year. Each quilt block has twelve panels memorializing AIDS victims. Now stored in Atlanta, the over 5900 block quilt is a reminder of the 36 million people who have died of AIDS world-wide to date.

annotations.title: Labyrinth / Chi Rho
annotations.text:
The labyrinth is an ancient symbolic form, developed in medieval French cathedrals into a walkable floor design. A single winding path leads from the edge to the center; symbolic of the wayward, but unbroken, path of the individual soul toward Christ. The practice was revived here by Canon Lauren Artress, founder of Veriditas (an international labyrinth group) as a means of focusing the walker on spiritual growth and healing. The design, adopted from the ca. 1220 Chartres Cathedral labyrinth in France, was first walked on canvas here (1991) followed by a carpet version, and the present pavement version (2007). Weekly yoga classes begun here now fill the building.

Placed at the center of the nave floor, linking the old and new parts of the Cathedral, is the brass Chi Rho (pronounced “kye-row”) or Greek “X” and “P” (the English “CH” and “R” of “CHRIST”). Here Bishop James Pike traced the letters with his crozier staff, consecrating the completed Grace Cathedral in 1964.

annotations.title: Concrete and Steel
annotations.text:
The use of raw concrete and steel for the Grace Cathedral fabric is daring and unusual, but the 1906 earthquake made structural strength necessary. Similarly concrete cathedrals are found in New Zealand, Colombia, Ecuador etc. along the seismically-active Pacific “Ring of Fire.” The first part of the cathedral was built of riveted steel lattices, beams and rebar (1927-1943), and the last portion of clustered steel rebar and beams (1960-1964). In both cases, wooden and plaster forms were built up around the steel framework and semi-liquid concrete poured into them, accumulating pour by pour, to the rooftops.

On the exterior, unadorned concrete was chosen for its contemporary texture and given a more weathered appearance by bush-hammering. The use of concrete required a simplification of much exterior architectural detail, resulting in a unified and somewhat monumental design. Concrete was poured into prepared wooden forms for the walls, and prepared plaster or latex molds for the detailed areas. Grace Cathedral is the nation’s, and probably the world’s, largest poured-in-place all reinforced concrete Gothic-style church building with a raw concrete exterior. Individual pours are clearly visible in places like these nave piers.

annotations.title: East Rose Window
annotations.text:
The name rose refers to the rose-like shape and petal-like tracery design. The window is in faceted glass, a French stained glass invention of the 1920s. Inch-thick glass bricks are chipped or faceted on their interior surfaces and set into reinforced cement, creating translucent ‘mosaics’ of colored glass in wall-like panels. There is no painting on the glass surface, and the ratio of glass to cement (or epoxy) surface area in a faceted glass window is under 50 percent. The window is by Gabriel Loire of Chartres, France, one of the leading French faceted glass artists of the last century, but uses a theme originally chosen by Charles Connick.

In semi-abstract form, the window, The Canticle of the Sun, shows natural symbols from St. Francis’ famous poem (1224-5), the oldest known poem in colloquial Italian, and originally set to music. The poem is a paean to the “most high omnipotent good Lord” celebrating the splendor and loving sustenance of the Creator and creation. In the center is Sir Brother Sun, and above it, the Chi-Rho symbol, linking Christ, the dawn, and light. Circling clockwise in the borders are Sister Moon and Stars (top), fruits and flowers of our Sister Mother Earth (lower right), Sister Water (right base), Brother Fire (lower left), and Brother Wind and Air with two soaring birds (upper left), and Sister Bodily Death (right center). A hammer and glass shards form the artist’s emblem (top left). Loire subtitled the window The Creation. The window faces the morning sunrise. It is floodlit from inside every evening. The window is 25 feet (8 m.) in diameter and has 109 segments and nearly 3800 pieces of glass. It is the largest rose window in the far western United States.

annotations.title: Einstein Window
annotations.text:
The faceted glass series by Gabriel Loire is devoted to 20th century Americans whose achievements were rooted in and sustained by God’s grace. Symbolic shapes surround each figure. This window features Einstein's famous
E = mc2 formula. The Human Endeavor series also includes Justice Thurgood Marshall, astronaut John Glenn, and poet Robert Frost.

annotations.title: Bishop's Chair
annotations.text: The word ‘’cathedral’’ refers to the bishop’s chair, or ‘’cathedra’’ which makes the church the bishop’s official seat. Grace Cathedral is the cathedral church of the Episcopal Diocese of California, originally statewide in area, now comprising most of the San Francisco Bay Area counties. The Cathedral is administered by the dean and chapter, with the support of a board of trustees and the cathedral congregation.

annotations.title: The Main Organ
annotations.text:
Grace Cathedral’s 7466-pipe Aeolian-Skinner instrument, the Charles B. Alexander Memorial Organ (1934), is one of the first and finest American classic style organs, and is among the largest church organs in the West. Although listed as Opus 910A of Ernest M. Skinner, America’s greatest organ designer of the early 1900s, the Alexander organ was largely designed by Englishman G. Donald Harrison. Balancing Baroque and orchestral sounds by using a broad mix of pipes and stops, the American classic organ could accommodate the eclectic repertoire of church music that developed in the early 20th century, while also expressing the brighter and more crisp sounds of earlier styles.

When built, the organ had five divisions: Choir, Great, Swell, Solo and Pedal, and 6,077 pipes, and a 20-horsepower blower in the crypt of the Cathedral. Thanks to the sustained interest and generosity of Harrison and his successor Joseph S. Whiteford, additions and minor tonal alterations were made in 1952 and 1956, raising the total to 7,286 pipes.

The console, too, went through several incarnations. In 1968 the original console was replaced by Fratelli Ruffatti of Padua, Italy. The console was mobilized in 1984, so that it could be rolled onto the choir floor and turned to any position for concerts. An electrical “umbilical cord” links it to the organ’s mechanism. Edward M. Stout, Bay Area organ curator emeritus, now retired, worked with often-limited resources to restore and repair the great organ during his 42-year tenure. In 1998 Schoenstein created a new console with digital memory and combination action. Today, the organ is the fifth largest in California (by manuals and ranks) and the fiftieth-largest in the world.

annotations.title: Nativity Creche
annotations.text: Set into a wall niche, the Nativity Creche (left) is by Antonio Sanjuan Villalba of Valencia, Spain (1956). It shows the Holy Family and Angel Gabriel gathered around the newborn Christ Child. The wise men (magi) offer their gifts as shepherds approach with humbler offerings. The ruined farm shed symbolizes the old order. The scene was carved from Swedish birchwood.

annotations.title: William Ingraham Kip
annotations.text:
William I. Kip (1811-1893), was the first Episcopalean Bishop of California, and served at Grace Church, which predated Grace Cathedral before it was destroyed in the 1906 fire. Kip had pondered the idea of a diocesan cathedral, but passed away before the fire presented the opportunity.

In 1865, Bishop Kip sat for this bust by the noted American sculptor William H. Rinehart (1825-1874). The bust, gift of the bishop’s descendants in 1984, is placed at the bishop’s correct standing height on a levanto marble base. A Kip family descendant married into the Koch family. A small break on the collar was made ca. 1946 by a toy thrown by the mischievous younger Koch brothers (the now famed twin financiers Bill and David) in whose parents’ Kansas City house the piece then stood.

annotations.title: Ghiberti Doors
annotations.text: These doors are replicas of gilded bronze doors by Florentine Renaissance sculptor Lorenzo Ghiberti, made for the Florence Cathedral Baptistry from 1425 to 1452. The originals are now in the cathedral museum there. Bronze expert Bruno Bearzi made molds of the original doors before World War II, and hid them from the Germans. In the 1960s he made replica doors from the molds, and Grace Cathedral obtained them. The doors are open on special occasions.

annotations.title: Interfaith Outdoor Labyrinth
annotations.text:
Like its indoor nave counterpart, it is a reproduction of the labyrinth at Chartres Cathedral. It is at 94% scale, and is 39.5 feet diameter with a path 810 feet long. Design differences from the Chartres original are the tightly curved, rather than sharp-cornered, ends of the straight-path segments, and slightly extended border cusps. The northeast/southwest orientation, while similar to that at Chartres, serves here to make the entry path easily accessible to visitors. A terrazzo original, built here in 1995, was the oldest outdoor labyrinth on a cathedral close.

Due to leak issues, it was rebuilt in granite in 2013 to the same design, but different colors. The path is of pink-grey Lac du Bonnet biotite granite from southern Manitoba, Canada. The path color echoes the color used in the nearby courtyard fountain and pavement design borders.

annotations.title: Carillon Bells
annotations.text: The north tower, the Singing Tower, houses the English-made carillon of 44 bells. The largest bell weighs 6 tons. Dr. Nathaniel Coulson, English-born San Francisco dentist and realtor gave the tower and bells. The carillon was loaned to the 1939-1940 Golden Gate Exposition on Treasure Island before installation here. Many bells have names reflecting the city’s religious diversity.

annotations.title: Cathedral Flêche (Spire)
annotations.text: Made of steel and lead-coated copper, the cathedral's flêche (from the French word for arrow) is the tallest in the west and the fourth tallest in the United States, rising 117 feet from the main roof ridge to 540 feet above sea level. The gilded steel cross at the top measures 8 feet wide by 13 feet tall and is in an elaborate floral style with leaves and flowers. The eight wyvern grotesques (not gargoyles) around the lantern portion serve as symbolic “holy pit bulls” warding off evil forces from the Cathedral and city. The flêche is floodlit every evening.
